### Consonants

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| **Affricate** |  | tɕ · dʒ |  |  |  |  |
| **Sibilant fricative** | s |  |  |  |  |  |

Where symbols share a cell, the voiceless ones come first and the voiced follow the dot. Secondary articulation (ʷ ʲ ˠ ˤ) and length (ː) stay in the cell of the plain sound.

### Vowels

| | Front | Back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Close** | i iː iᴖ | u uː uᴖ uːᴖ |
| **Close-mid** | e eː eᴖ | o oᴖ |
| **Open-mid** | ɛ |  |
| **Open** | a |  |

Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: long vowels uː eː uːᴖ iː. Nasality: no nasal vowels.

**Sounds outside the human voice** (house and VoQS symbols, `planet/language/data/symbols.tsv`):

- **ᴖ** (a second simultaneous voice (syrinx)): uᴖ, iᴖ, eᴖ, uːᴖ, oᴖ. Symbol table: second simultaneous source (syrinx two-voice; ᴖ U+1D16).

Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 33%, CVC 29%, V 4%, VC 3%. At most 1 consonant(s) before the vowel and 1 after it.
Stress falls on the first syllable. The IPA on this page marks it with ˈ before the stressed syllable.
Core words average 1.41 syllables (2.9 sounds); 34% of words share their form with another word.

### Allophony

This output records no allophones (the engine stores sounds as phonemes only).

### Phonological rules

Rules the language applies today, in order. A new sound change starts as a rule applying across words; as it ages it narrows to words, then to word-making, and in the end dies, leaving its alternations in single words.

| # | rule | applies | since | example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | k͡p → ɡ͡b, s → z, t → d, tɕ → dʑ / _[+voice −son] | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~6 kyr ago | e˦s + dʒu˦ → e˦zdʒu˦ 'eye + flesh or meat (compound)' |
| 2 | s → ∅ / _# | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~3.5 kyr ago | – |
| 3 | a → ∅, e → ∅, eː → ∅, eᴖ → ∅ / _# (apocope) | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~3 kyr ago | i˦ + -i˦ → i˦ 'arm or hand-agent' |
| 4 | x → ∅ / _C (with compensatory lengthening) | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2.5 kyr ago | – |
| 5 | d → t, dʒ → tʃ, ɡ͡b → k͡p / _# | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2.5 kyr ago | – |
| 6 | l → r / C_ | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2 kyr ago | i˦n + lɛ˨ → i˦nrɛ˨ 'be alive + night (compound)' |
| 7 | d → ∅, dʒ → ∅, j → ∅, k͡p → ∅ / C_# (final cluster simplification: the last of two final consonants lost) | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | – |
| 8 | a → ∅, e → ∅, eː → ∅, eᴖ → ∅ / C_# [−stress] | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | i˦n + -i˦ → i˦n 'be alive-agent' |

Lately dead: S019 (crowded out by younger rules, 1 kyr ago); S143 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S197 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S013 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S102 (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago); S054 (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago).

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** n ‹n› · nʲ ‹ny› · ŋ ‹ng› · t ‹t› · tʲ ‹ty› · d ‹d› · k͡p ‹kp› · ɡ͡b ‹gb› · ʔ ‹'› · tɕ ‹ć› ‹c› · dʒ ‹j› · s ‹s› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l ‹l› · ʎ ‹ly› · r ‹rr› · rʲ ‹rry›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · iᴖ ‹iwh› · iː ‹ii› · u ‹u› · uᴖ ‹uwh› · uː ‹uu› · uːᴖ ‹uuwh› · e ‹e› · eᴖ ‹ewh› · eː ‹ee› · o ‹o› · oᴖ ‹owh› · ɛ ‹ẹ› ‹e› · a ‹a›

Tones are written over the vowel: low grave à, mid unmarked a, high acute á, rising caron ǎ, falling circumflex â (Yoruba-style).

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; noun before the numeral; relative clause before the noun. Overall it is head-final.
It has no definite article, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), no grammatical number, gender by animacy.
Verbs mark progressive; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a verb form. Verbs agree with the subject by suffixes and with the object by suffixes.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; an inclusive/exclusive 'we' distinction; serial verbs; verb reduplication; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words left in place; a decimal counting base.
Measured morphology: 18 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.3 (0 free word … 3 fused), 24 paradigm cells, 14 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (ri˨), 'at' (la˨nuː˨), 'with' (sa˧) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns fall into genders by animacy: class 1 for things, a prefix (u˦ᴖw, from 'stone'); class 2 for living beings, a prefix (lu˦, from 'person'); class 3 for lands, qualities and abstractions, a clitic before the noun (la˦w, from 'name').

| *u˦ᴖw-nʲi˨* |
| --- |
| INAN-water |

‘water’

| *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* |
| --- |
| ANIM-dog |

‘dog’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Progressive (PROG): a clitic after the verb (u˦ᴖnʲi˨w; wu˦ᴖnʲi˨w after a back or rounded vowel; from 'at'). Unmarked: past, future, perfective, habitual (left to context).

| *a˦ʔu˦ᴖ=wu˦ᴖnʲi˨w* |
| --- |
| go=PROG |

‘(it) is going’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 2PL: a clitic after the verb (i˦u˨ᴖw; wi˦u˨ᴖw after a back or rounded vowel; from 'you'); 1PL.INCL: a suffix (ʔu˦ᴖj, from 'we'). Subject pronouns are dropped when the marker is there. No marker yet for 1SG, 2SG, 3SG, 1PL, 3PL (zero). The inclusive 'we' has a marker of its own (1PL.INCL); 1PL is the exclusive.

| *a˦ʔu˦ᴖ=wi˦u˨ᴖw* |
| --- |
| go=2PL |

‘you all go’

| *a˦ʔu˦ᴖ-ʔu˦ᴖj* |
| --- |
| go-1PL.INCL |

‘we (you and I) go’

**Object agreement.** Verbs also agree with the object: 1SG.OBJ: a clitic after the verb (ɛ˦; jɛ˦ after a front or central vowel; from 'I'); 2SG.OBJ: a clitic after the verb (i˦u˨ᴖw; ji˦u˨ᴖw after a front or central vowel; from 'thou'); 1PL.OBJ: a clitic after the verb (i˦lu˨ᴖw; ji˦lu˨ᴖw after a front or central vowel; from 'we'); 2PL.OBJ: a clitic after the verb (tɛ˦lʔi˦, from 'you'); 3PL.OBJ: a clitic after the verb (rʲi˦ʔu˦ᴖn, from 'they'). No marker yet for 3SG.OBJ.

| *e˦tɕi˨=jɛ˦* |
| --- |
| see=1SG.OBJ |

‘he/she sees me’

| *e˦tɕi˨=ji˦u˨ᴖw* |
| --- |
| see=2SG.OBJ |

‘he/she sees you’

| *e˦tɕi˨=ji˦lu˨ᴖw* |
| --- |
| see=1PL.OBJ |

‘he/she sees us’

**Negation.** Negation uses the word for 'not' (nu˧), preverbal.

| *ɛ˦* | *u˦ᴖw-k͡po˦* | *nu˧* | *wa˨* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | INAN-milk | NEG | drink |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a marker on the verb. Question words stay where the questioned phrase would stand: who nu˨ᴖ, what u˦, where u˦ʔ, when u˦ᴖn, how i˧.

| *i˦u˨ᴖw* | *u˦ᴖw-ra˦k͡pu˦ᴖʔu˦ʔ* | *u˦ᴖ-wa˧* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | INAN-thunder | Q-hear |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *lu˦-we˧lu˨ᴖj* | *u˦* | *lu˦-k͡pi˨u˨* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-child | what | ANIM-bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *lu˦-wi˧ra˧* | *nʲa˨* |
| --- | --- |
| ANIM-fish | eat |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. 'Having' is said with 'with' ('my mother is with a boat').

| *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* |
| --- | --- |
| ANIM-man | ANIM-dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *ɛ˦* | *lu˦-na˨n* | *u˦ᴖw-nʲi˨ru˨ᴖj* | *sa˧* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | ANIM-mother | INAN-boat | with |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause before the noun, no relativizer.

| *a˦lu˨ᴖ* | *lu˦-na˨n* |
| --- | --- |
| dance | ANIM-woman |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** There is no copula: a predicate noun stands beside its subject.

| *lu˦-nʲi˨nnʲi˨n* | *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖk͡p* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-that | ANIM-man | ANIM-merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *u˦ᴖw-nʲi˨* | *tɕi˨n* |
| --- | --- |
| INAN-water | cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Pronouns.** 'We' has two forms: inclusive u˦ᴖe˦n (you and I, the hearer among us) and exclusive i˦lu˨ᴖw (we, but not you).

| *u˦ᴖe˦n* |
| --- |
| 1PL.INCL |

‘we (you included)’

| *i˦lu˨ᴖw* |
| --- |
| 1PL.EXCL |

‘we (not you)’

| *u˦ᴖe˦n* | *lu˦-wi˧ra˧* | *nʲa˨-ʔu˦ᴖj* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1PL.INCL | ANIM-fish | eat-1PL.INCL |

‘We (you and I) eat the fish.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done again and again, or by many (ITER), by copying the stem's first consonant and vowel before it.

| *a˦-a˦ʔu˦ᴖ* |
| --- |
| ITER-go |

‘(an action done again and again, or by many)’

| *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *lu˦-wi˧ra˧* | *lu˦-ta˧-ta˧* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-man | ANIM-fish | ANIM-ITER-hit |

‘The man hits the fish again and again.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *lu˦-wi˧ra˧* | *u˦* | *su˦k͡p* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-man | ANIM-fish | take | come |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 13 below)

| *k͡pu˧j* | *a˦ʔu˦ᴖ* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** No dative: a serial construction, 'take the thing, give (it to) the person'.

| *lu˦-na˨n* | *lu˦-wi˧ra˧* | *u˦* | *lu˦-we˧lu˨ᴖj* | *a˧ri˧w* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-woman | ANIM-fish | take | ANIM-child | give |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is a˦l and a hundred is k͡pa˧ni˧l.

| *u˦ᴖwʔa˦l* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *u˦ᴖwu˨ᴖ* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *sa˧ŋu˧ŋi˧n* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Concord.** The noun's class marker is copied onto demonstratives and adjectives and the verb (subject concord) (agreement in class, as in Bantu and in Indo-European gender).

| *lu˦-nʲi˨nnʲi˨n* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* | *lu˦-wo˨na˨* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-that | ANIM-dog | ANIM-big |

‘that big dog’

**Linking clauses.** Clauses are linked by complementizer ('that') (COMP): a clitic after the verb phrase (nu˨ᴖ, from the relativizer marker).

| *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* | *lu˦-lo˦˨rɛ˦˨t=nu˨ᴖ* | *lu˦-wi˧ŋu˧s* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-man | ANIM-dog | ANIM-sleep=COMP | ANIM-say |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 17 below)

**Topic and focus.** Topic and focus are marked: topic (TOP): a clitic after the noun phrase (u˦n; ju˦n after a front or central vowel; from 'if').

| *lu˦-wi˧ra˧=ju˦n* | *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *lu˦-nʲa˨* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-fish=TOP | ANIM-man | ANIM-eat |

‘The fish, the man eats it.’ (sentence 18 below)

**Word shapes.** Some markers sound the same: 2PL and 2SG.OBJ are both i˦u˨ᴖw (context tells them apart).

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' i˦ᴖnʲi˨w (near) and 'that' nʲi˨nnʲi˨n (far).

| *lu˦-wi˦ᴖnʲi˨w* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* |
| --- | --- |
| ANIM-this | ANIM-dog |

‘this dog’

| *lu˦-nʲi˨nnʲi˨n* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* |
| --- | --- |
| ANIM-that | ANIM-dog |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| *lu˦-we˦k͡pu˨j* | *o˨na˨* | *lu˦-wu˦ᴖn* | *la˧* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ANIM-man | big | ANIM-dog | exceed |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 19 below)

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are a short sentence about the birth run together (as Yoruba *Babatunde* 'father has returned'); the byname is an epithet after the name. The tradition goes back to the aarakocra proto-language.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **Wewsukp** | /wɛ˦wsu˦k͡p/ | 'the rain came' | old | Wewsukp 'the rain came': wew 'rain' + sukp 'come'; an old name, coined in d292 4.0 kyr ago as Wewsukp |
| **Orruun** | /o˦ruː˦˨n/ | 'the people sing' | old | Orruun 'the people sing': orruyekpuy 'people' + un 'sing'; an old name, coined in d292 4.0 kyr ago as Orru·un |
| **Iiy** | /iː˦j/ | 'the war is over' | old | Iiy 'the war is over': ii 'war' + iy 'finish'; an old name, coined in d292 4.0 kyr ago as Ii·iy |
| **Rraluy** | /ra˦lu˦j/ | 'the sun rose' | new | Rraluy 'the sun rose': rraluy 'sun' + kpa 'rise'; coined from today's words |
| **Nan·yal** | /na˨nja˦˨l/ | 'mother laughed' | new | Nan·yal 'mother laughed': nan 'mother' + yal 'laugh'; coined from today's words |
| **Lilut** | /li˦˨lu˧t/ | 'God knows' | new | Lilut 'God knows': li 'god' + lud 'know'; coined from today's words |
| **Wewsukp Ikpiy** | /wɛ˦wsu˦k͡p i˦k͡pi˨j/ | 'the rain came, the black' | epithet | ikpiy 'black', a byname |
| **Orruun Ikpiy** | /o˦ruː˦˨n i˦k͡pi˨j/ | 'the people sing, the black' | epithet | ikpiy 'black', a byname |

**Settlements.** **Ali'is** /a˦li˦ʔi˦s/ (village, 511): 'the black field'; named by the human (d561.1) who founded it lately, kept as heard.

## Gods and liturgy

**Faith.** The fire schism of the aarakocra of the north of Sothasor, founded 14 kyr ago ago, held by 6 languages.

| god | name | IPA | meaning | the same name elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| god of mountain and forest | **Nuakp** | /nu˨a˨k͡p/ | 'the lord' | — |
| god of sky and storm | **Iw** | /i˦w/ | 'the one who sees' | — |
| god of sea and rain | **Luwhee** | /lu˨ᴖeː˨/ | 'River' | Laen (aarakocra 34) |
| god of hunt and fertility | **E'uwhw** | /ɛ˦ʔu˦ᴖw/ | 'chief of the hunt' | Ae'uwhw (aarakocra 34) |

How the first name came about: taken by d292 from d53, 5.5 kyr ago; 'the lord' (a title in place of the name (the old name avoided); it replaced the old name u˦ᴖl 'the one who stands') in d292, 5 kyr ago.

**Liturgy.** The faith's rites are kept in the aarakocra speech of aarakocra 8 as it was 5 kyr ago ago, frozen since (as Latin, Sanskrit or Ge'ez are).

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.

## Relatives and intelligibility

Shared-origin share: the share of core-100 meanings whose words go back to the same etymon (true cognates, and loans between the two). Intelligibility is the engine's estimate (blind cognates, how far the cognates have drifted, and grammar differences).
